questions.stem: In communication, decoding is the process of:
options: interpreting a message to work out what it means
putting thoughts into words or signals to send
choosing the channel through which a message is sent
repeating a message so that it is remembered
questions.explanation: The sender codes (encodes) a message into words and signals, and the receiver decodes it by interpreting its meaning. Misunderstandings occur when the message is decoded differently from how it was intended.

questions.stem: Non-verbal communication is best defined as:
options: the grammar and vocabulary of a language
any message sent through a phone or computer
sending and receiving messages without words
communication that is written instead of spoken
questions.explanation: Non-verbal communication includes facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact, touch, use of space, voice qualities and appearance, all of which carry meaning without words.

questions.stem: A friend says 'I'm fine' with a flat voice, slumped shoulders and no eye contact. Most people would believe:
options: the non-verbal signals, which suggest she is not fine
the words, because spoken language is always accurate
neither, because mixed messages cannot be decoded
the words, because non-verbal cues have no meaning
questions.explanation: When verbal and non-verbal messages conflict, people tend to trust the non-verbal cues, which are harder to control. Here they suggest she is not fine.

questions.stem: At around 6 months of age, infants typically begin to:
options: babble, repeating sounds such as 'bababa'
speak in full sentences of several words
use two-word phrases such as 'more milk'
read simple words printed in picture books
questions.explanation: Babbling, repeating consonant-vowel sounds, typically begins around 6 months. First words usually appear around 12 months and two-word phrases around 18 to 24 months.

questions.stem: A toddler says 'Daddy go car' instead of 'Daddy is going in the car'. This is an example of:
options: babbling
paralinguistic speech
an emblem gesture
telegraphic speech
questions.explanation: Telegraphic speech uses key content words and leaves out small words such as 'is' and 'the', like an old telegram. It appears as children move beyond the two-word stage.

questions.stem: Children around the world pass through similar stages of language development at similar ages, whatever language they learn. Which view does this support?
options: Language development depends entirely on formal schooling
Humans have an inborn capacity for learning language
Language is learned only by imitating adults' speech
Language is learned only through rewards for correct words
questions.explanation: Similar stages across cultures support Chomsky's idea of an inborn language acquisition device. Imitation and reinforcement also play a part, but cannot alone explain the shared pattern.

questions.stem: Research by Willis and Todorov (2006) found that people form judgements such as trustworthiness from a face after seeing it for:
options: about one hour
about one-tenth of a second
about one full minute
about ten minutes
questions.explanation: Willis and Todorov found that judgements made after a 100 millisecond exposure to a face were very similar to those made with no time limit, showing how quickly first impressions form.

questions.stem: Asch gave people a list of traits describing a stranger. When 'warm' was swapped for 'cold' in the middle of the list, overall impressions changed greatly. This shows that:
options: some traits are central and shape the whole impression
the last trait in a list always has the most influence
impressions are formed only from non-verbal information
impressions are not affected by the information given
questions.explanation: Changing one central trait altered the whole impression, showing that some characteristics strongly organise how we see a person.

questions.stem: Asch also found that a person described first by positive traits and then negative ones was rated more favourably than when the order was reversed. This is:
options: the halo effect
telegraphic speech
the primacy effect
the recency effect
questions.explanation: The primacy effect is the greater influence of information received first. Early information shapes how later information is interpreted.

questions.stem: Which is the best advice for creating a positive first impression at a job interview?
options: Stand as close as possible to show that you are friendly
Speak very quickly so you can give as much detail as possible
Make suitable eye contact, smile and sit in an open posture
Avoid all eye contact and keep your arms tightly folded
questions.explanation: Appropriate eye contact, smiling and an open posture signal confidence and interest. Crossed arms and avoiding eye contact can appear defensive or uninterested.

questions.stem: To maintain a positive impression over time, which matters most?
options: Changing appearance and behaviour as often as possible to stay interesting
Relying only on the first impression, which cannot be changed afterwards
Avoiding non-verbal communication so that only words are judged
Later behaviour staying consistent with the first impression
questions.explanation: Impressions are maintained when later behaviour is consistent with the first impression. Inconsistent behaviour leads people to revise their judgements.

questions.stem: Darwin (1872) argued that facial expressions of emotion:
options: evolved and are shared across humans and some animals
are learned separately in each culture from parents
have no link to the emotions a person feels inside
appear only once children have learned to speak
questions.explanation: In The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, Darwin argued that expressions evolved because they helped survival and are therefore universal.

questions.stem: Which six emotions did Ekman and Friesen identify as having universally recognised facial expressions?
options: joy, love, anger, fear, envy, embarrassment
happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, disgust
happiness, sadness, anger, jealousy, pride, shame
happiness, boredom, anger, fear, guilt, disgust
questions.explanation: Ekman and Friesen identified happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise and disgust as basic emotions whose expressions are recognised across cultures.

questions.stem: Ekman and Friesen found that people of the Fore group in Papua New Guinea, who had little contact with outside media, correctly matched faces to emotional stories. Why was this group important?
options: They could not have learned the expressions from Western films or photos
They had been trained to recognise expressions in a laboratory setting
They spoke the same language as the researchers who carried out the study
They showed that expressions differ completely from culture to culture
questions.explanation: Because the Fore had little exposure to Western media, their accurate recognition suggests the expressions are universal rather than learned from outside cultures.

questions.stem: Students in two countries watch an upsetting film. Alone, both groups show disgust; with an authority figure present, one group smiles politely. This difference reflects:
options: paralinguistic features
proxemic zones
cultural display rules
universal facial expressions
questions.explanation: Display rules are cultural norms about when and how emotions should be shown. The underlying expressions are universal, but cultures differ in when they are displayed.

questions.stem: Kinesics is the study of:
options: voice qualities such as pitch
body movements, gestures and posture
the use of personal space and distance
touch in communication
questions.explanation: Birdwhistell coined the term kinesics for the study of body movement as communication, including gestures, posture and facial movement. Personal space is proxemics and touch is haptics.

questions.stem: A thumbs-up gesture means 'good' in Australia but is offensive in some other countries. Gestures like this, with a direct verbal meaning, are called:
options: adaptors
regulators
emblems
illustrators
questions.explanation: Emblems are gestures with a specific meaning that can replace words, and their meanings vary between cultures. Illustrators accompany speech, adaptors relieve tension, and regulators manage conversation.

questions.stem: A person absent-mindedly twists her hair while waiting for an exam to start. This gesture is:
options: an adaptor
an emblem
an illustrator
a regulator
questions.explanation: Adaptors are often unconscious movements, such as fidgeting or touching oneself, that help manage feelings like anxiety or boredom.

questions.stem: Nodding and leaning forward to signal 'keep talking' during a conversation are examples of:
options: affect displays
regulators
emblems
adaptors
questions.explanation: Regulators are non-verbal signals that control the flow of conversation, such as nodding, eye contact and pausing to signal turn-taking.

questions.stem: Hewes proposed a theory about the role of gestures in human communication. What did he suggest?
options: Gestures are identical in every culture because they are all inborn
Gestures are used only by young children before they can speak
Spoken language may have grown out of earlier gestural communication
Gestures have no meaning unless they are accompanied by spoken words
questions.explanation: Hewes argued that human language may have begun with gestures, which were later replaced or joined by speech. Gestures still accompany and support spoken language.

questions.stem: A student sits with arms folded, body turned away and legs crossed away from the speaker. This posture is most likely to be read as:
options: relaxed and friendly
closed and defensive
open and welcoming
dominant and confident
questions.explanation: Folded arms and turning away form a closed posture, often interpreted as defensive or uninterested. An open posture, with uncrossed limbs facing the other person, signals interest.

questions.stem: Paralinguistics refers to:
options: how something is said, such as tone, pitch and pace
the words and grammar used to form a sentence
the distance people keep from one another
the meaning of hand gestures in a culture
questions.explanation: Paralinguistic features are the vocal qualities that accompany speech, including tone, pitch, volume, speed, pauses and sounds like 'um'. Crystal studied these features.

questions.stem: A student says 'Great, another test' in a sarcastic tone. The listener understands she is not pleased. This shows the role of:
options: proxemics
haptics
kinesics
paralinguistics
questions.explanation: Tone of voice changes the meaning of the words, here signalling sarcasm. This is paralinguistic communication.

questions.stem: Mehrabian's research is often summarised as '7% words, 38% tone of voice, 55% body language'. Why is it wrong to apply this to all communication?
options: It applied to judging feelings when words and cues conflicted
It applied only to written letters rather than face-to-face speaking
It applied only to young children who had not yet learned to speak
It applied only to people speaking a second language they were learning
questions.explanation: Mehrabian studied how people judge feelings and attitudes when words and non-verbal cues are inconsistent. He did not claim words carry only 7% of meaning in all communication.

questions.stem: Proxemics is the study of:
options: how people use space and distance
how people use touch
how people use eye contact
how people use voice
questions.explanation: Hall introduced proxemics, the study of how people use personal space and physical distance in communication.

questions.stem: In Hall's model, which zone is usually reserved for close friends and family, within about 45 cm?
options: public distance
intimate distance
personal distance
social distance
questions.explanation: Hall's intimate zone, up to about 45 cm, is for close relationships. Personal distance (about 45 cm to 1.2 m) is for friends and conversation, social distance for business, and public distance for speeches.

questions.stem: A teacher speaks to a whole school assembly from a stage. In Hall's model, this is:
options: social distance
personal distance
intimate distance
public distance
questions.explanation: Public distance, beyond about 3.6 m, is used for addressing groups or audiences. Social distance (about 1.2 to 3.6 m) suits formal interactions such as a meeting.

questions.stem: A visitor from a culture where people stand close when talking keeps stepping towards an Australian, who keeps stepping back. Which explanation is best?
options: Norms for personal space differ between cultures
One of them has poor eyesight and needs to be closer
Personal space zones are identical across all cultures
The visitor is deliberately trying to be aggressive
questions.explanation: Hall showed that comfortable distances vary between cultures. People from high-contact cultures tend to stand closer than people from lower-contact cultures.

questions.stem: On an almost empty bus, a stranger sits right next to a passenger, who soon moves to another seat. Which explanation does Hall's work suggest?
options: The stranger was inside a zone of personal space usually kept for friends
The stranger was too far away to be heard in normal conversation
Personal space matters only in public speaking and not in daily life
People everywhere prefer to sit as close as possible to strangers
questions.explanation: When a stranger enters the personal or intimate zone without need, people often feel uncomfortable and restore distance. On a nearly empty bus, sitting right next to someone breaks the usual norm.

questions.stem: Haptics is the study of communication through:
options: facial expression
tone of voice
clothing
touch
questions.explanation: Haptics refers to touch in communication, such as handshakes, hugs and pats on the back. Its meaning depends on the relationship, context and culture.

questions.stem: Why might a firm handshake be appropriate in an Australian job interview, but a hug inappropriate?
options: Handshakes are inborn, while hugs are learned behaviours
Touch is never used in formal Australian settings at all
Norms for touch depend on the relationship and setting
Touch has the same meaning in every type of situation
questions.explanation: Haptic norms vary by relationship, setting and culture. A handshake is a conventional formal greeting, while a hug suggests a closer relationship.

questions.stem: During a conversation, a speaker looks away while thinking and then looks back at the listener when finishing. This use of gaze helps to:
options: replace the words of the message entirely
regulate turn-taking in the conversation
show the speaker's dislike of the listener
increase the personal space between them
questions.explanation: Gaze helps manage conversations: speakers often look away while planning and look back to signal they are finishing, inviting the listener to respond.

questions.stem: A candidate wears a suit to an interview for an office job. Which aspect of non-verbal communication is she using?
options: paralinguistics
appearance
proxemics
haptics
questions.explanation: Appearance, including clothing, grooming and accessories, communicates information about a person and influences first impressions.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about non-verbal communication is best supported by research?
options: Basic facial expressions are largely universal; gestures and space vary
All non-verbal communication is learned and differs completely between cultures
All non-verbal communication is inborn and identical in every culture
Non-verbal communication is universal only in adults, not in children
questions.explanation: Ekman's research supports universal recognition of basic facial expressions, while emblems, display rules, personal space and touch norms differ across cultures. Communication is partly universal and partly cultural.

questions.stem: A national flag is a symbol. What makes it a symbol rather than a natural sign?
options: Its meaning depends only on the colour of the cloth
Its meaning is agreed and learned within a culture
Its meaning comes from a natural cause and effect
Its meaning is understood the same way by everyone
questions.explanation: A symbol stands for something by convention, so its meaning must be learned. A natural sign, such as smoke indicating fire, is linked to its meaning by cause and effect.

questions.stem: Chartrand and Bargh found that people whose posture and mannerisms were subtly copied by a partner liked that partner more. What does this suggest about non-verbal communication in relationships?
options: Unconscious mimicry helps build rapport and liking
Copying others always makes them feel uncomfortable
Liking depends only on what people say to each other
Rapport is built mainly through touch, not posture
questions.explanation: This is the chameleon effect: people unconsciously mimic one another, and being mimicked increases liking and smooths interactions. Non-verbal cues such as mirroring, gaze and posture help build and maintain relationships.
